sections.h2: Which counter handles which tax question
sections.html:
Property tax questions in New Castle go to one of three offices. Pick by topic: what the house is worth, paying this year's bill, or a bill that is already late.

Where to go in Henry County
OfficeWhere and whenUse it for
PVA23 South Property Road, New Castle, KY 40050 (mail to P.O. Box 11), (502) 845-5740, open 8 to 4:30Assessments, ownership records, homestead applications
Sheriff(502) 845-2909Sends and collects the current bill
County Clerk27 South Property Road, P.O. Box 615, (502) 845-5705, weekdays 8 to 4, closed noon to 1Late bills and deed recordings, with eRecording

The PVA's website links to a bill search run from the sheriff's records.

January 1 is the date for both the assessment and the tax owner. If you buy in June, that year's state bill still goes out in the seller's name, and the new owner appears the following year. The office tries to mail a copy to the new owner from the recorded deed. A buyer who gets nothing can phone the sheriff.

Henry County is a farm and commuter county in north central Kentucky, and it has served as an exurb of the Louisville area since the 1990s. New Castle holds the courthouse, and Eminence is the largest city. Population grew from 15,678 in the 2020 census to an estimated 16,447 in 2025, up 4.9 percent.

Of 6,883 housing units, 76.3 percent are owner-occupied. A typical owned home is valued at $197,900, and typical gross rent is $895. About 89.5 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, so your likely buyer is moving in from elsewhere. Commutes average 30.5 minutes, a selling point for anyone driving toward Louisville. Henry County Schools and the Eminence Independent district both serve the county, and a listing should say which one an address falls in.

Residents 65 and over make up about 20.9 percent of the county, the group the homestead reduction below is written for.

sections.h2: Who can ask the appeals board to change an assessment
sections.html:
Officials can start a review as well as owners. KRS 133.120 lets the board of assessment appeals change a value if the county judge/executive, a city mayor using the county assessment, or a school superintendent asks in writing and names the parcel. The Department of Revenue can make the same recommendation.

If you are the owner, start with a PVA conference. Then file a written petition at the county clerk's office by the workday after inspection ends. Hearings begin 25 to 35 days after inspection closes (KRS 133.030), and the board usually wraps up inside five days.

  • Collect land and building descriptions, insurance policies, construction costs, listings and loan papers.
  • If the board weighs a higher value, you get a notice and a date to protest.
  • A taxpayer who listed their own parcel at fair cash value may ask the board to look at a neighbor's apparent under-assessment, in writing and with comparable sales or cost data.
  • The board can't reopen values across the board.

Keep paying while the appeal runs. Your payment is based on the value you claimed, and the sheriff bills any difference later with interest.

If you are 65 or older, or totally disabled, your primary residence can qualify for a reduction of $49,100 in assessed value for 2025 and 2026. File the application at the PVA's office.

Bring a birth certificate, license or passport as proof of age. A disability claim needs a federal or retirement-system classification and is renewed every year, with exceptions for service-connected disability and permanent Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems determinations.

If you sell, the exemption ends with your ownership. The buyer has to file their own application if they qualify, so mention it when you hand over the tax paperwork.

sections.h2: Clearing tax debt before you sell
sections.html:
Plan for the debt now. Whoever owned the house on January 1 owes that year's tax personally, and a delinquency lien under KRS 134.420 stays alive for eleven years even after the house changes hands.

Get a current-year payoff from the sheriff. For any year already late, go to the Henry County Clerk, whose website has a delinquent taxes link. Once claims reach the clerk, KRS 134.119 stacks on the sheriff's fee: ten percent of the tax and ten percent of the penalty. Avoiding that starts with the calendar in KRS 134.015, where paying by November 1 saves 2 percent and each late stage after December 31 costs 5 and then 10 percent.

Deed recording also runs through the clerk, and the seller's transfer tax under KRS 142.050 is collected there. Call the office for current charges.

The state calendar in KRS 134.015 rewards early payment. Pay by November 1 and you save 2 percent. After December 31, each late stage adds 5 percent and then 10 percent. Once the claim lands at the clerk, the sheriff's fee of ten percent of the tax and ten percent of the penalty is added on top.

That makes a payoff figure from the sheriff in October very different from one in March. If you are listing in the fall, paying the current bill before November 1 is a cheap way to take one open item off the title company's list. If you list in spring, call the sheriff first and the clerk second, because the file may have moved between them.

The sheriff is the right call for the current year, and the clerk is the right call once a bill is late. Write down the name of whoever you speak to and the date. If the two offices give different totals, ask the title company to request a written payoff from each, so the closing statement rests on paper and not on a phone call. Ask each office how long its figure stays good.

Expect the title company to ask the sheriff and the clerk for payoff figures. Tell them early who owned on January 1, because the old bill may still carry your name after the deed is recorded. Anything unpaid comes out of your proceeds at the table, and the title agent sends payment to the right office.

A cash sale moves faster only if the tax file is clean. A delinquent year with the clerk adds a payoff step, and a lender or title agent will not skip it. If you owe, call the clerk a week or two before closing for an updated number, then confirm with the title company which office it will pay.

Hold on to every letter the PVA or board sends about a value dispute. A buyer may ask whether an appeal is open, and you can answer with paperwork instead of memory.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Henry County, Kentucky?
faqs.a: The Henry County Sheriff, at (502) 845-2909. Delinquent bills go to the Henry County Clerk at (502) 845-5705.

faqs.q: Why does my Henry County bill name the previous owner?
faqs.a: Ownership is locked in on January 1. A purchase after that date leaves the bill under the former owner until the next calendar year.

faqs.q: What is the Henry County homestead amount?
faqs.a: It is $49,100 for assessment years 2025 and 2026, open to owners 65 or older or totally disabled through an application at the PVA.

faqs.q: Who besides the owner can seek a review of a Henry County value?
faqs.a: The county judge/executive, a city mayor, a school superintendent or the Department of Revenue, each by written recommendation naming the parcel.

faqs.q: Does an appeal stop my Henry County tax bill?
faqs.a: No. Pay tax on the value you claimed while the appeal runs, and expect a bill for any increase with interest.
